newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong journalist freed by China "surprised".
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong journalist freed by China "surprised".

text.p: HONG KONG, Jan 25 - A Hong Kong newspaper journalist who was paroled by China on Saturday after serving three years of a 12-year prison term for stealing state secrets returned to the British colony a surprised and happy man.
Xi Yang, 40, who had been a reporter for the Chinese-language Hong Kong newspaper Ming Pao, was released 157 days before the colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
He was greeted on arrival in the colony by colleagues who presented him with a large cake.
"I was surprised by the release," he said, adding that his health and spirits were fine.

Diplomats in Beijing welcomed Xi's release but were baffled because China has been tightening its grip on the media, calling on reporters to back the Communist Party's policies and give priority to what it termed "positive" reporting.
Xi's years in jail had clearly taken a toll.
He looked tired and grey-complexioned and was visibly overcome with emotion on occasions as he faced the media gathered at the Ming Pao offices.
His sister read out a letter from Xi's father in Beijing expressing the family's joy and relief.
"Xi Yang's parole was a surprise for me and I am extremely happy," his father, Xi Linsheng, said in the note.
"His early release is our family's dream," the note said. It expressed the Xi family's "heartfelt thanks to friends, Hong Kong people and those who cared for Xi Yang".
China's official news agency Xinhua said Xi was released on parole because he "showed signs of repentance".
Xi's collegues said they had been told his health had deteriorated while he was in prison.

He was released early on Saturday morning and visited his family in Beijing before flying to Hong Kong. Xi said he was too tired to think about his future and had not decided whether to return to journalism.
China jailed Xi for 12 years in March 1994 on charges of stealing state secrets about internal policies on interest rates and gold.
The severity of the sentence shocked Hong Kong reporters, already pessimistic about the prospects for a free press after the handover and triggered protests in the British colony.

His conviction had been seen as an attempt by Beijing to intimidate Hong Kong media before 1997 and to stop reporters from the colony uncovering news not published in the official Chinese media which serves as a tool of the Communist Party.
A clerk at China's central bank, Tian Ye, was jailed for 15 years for giving Xi information on Beijing's interest rate policy and plans for gold sales on the international market.
"I am delighted at the news that Mr Xi Yang has been released from prison and is now back in Hong Kong," the colony's governor, Chris Patten, said.

"His case has caused great anxiety and concenn to his family, his colleagues and the whole community. His release is very good news for Hong Kong as we approach the ChineseNNew Year (on February 7)," Patten added.
Separately, China and Hong Kong's outgoing colonial masters, Britain, are embroiled in a row over Beijing's plans to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover.
Pro-democracy activists have staged protests over the past week objecting to China's plans.
China insists the alterations would not weaken human rights protections in the territory after the handover.
